title: The Sultan of Al-Hind and His Son Mohammed
summary: In a magnificent coastal kingdom of India ruled Sultan Shams al-Din, whose only son, Prince Mohammed, grew up surrounded by velvet cushions, golden fans, and fawning courtiers. ...
keywords: story of a sultan of al-hind and his son mohammed
full_text:
In a magnificent coastal kingdom of India ruled Sultan Shams al-Din, whose only son, Prince Mohammed, grew up surrounded by velvet cushions, golden fans, and fawning courtiers. The young prince believed that bread grew on silver trays and that common laborers were born merely to serve kings.

Seeing his son's dangerous detachment, the Sultan summoned his guards one midnight, placed the sleeping prince on an ordinary merchant dhow sailing for the port of Surat, and commanded the captain:
'Leave him on the docks with nothing but a rough wool vest and five copper coins. Tell him the Sultan has disowned him until he returns with a purse filled with gold earned by his own sweat.'

Prince Mohammed awoke on the windy stone wharves of Surat, surrounded by shouting porters and smelling of salted fish. When he proclaimed his royal birth, the sailors laughed uproariously:
'A prince? Then carry this sack of peppercorns to the warehouse, Your Majesty, and earn two coppers for breakfast!'

Hunger soon conquered pride. His royal tunic tore, his soft hands blistered, and he spent his first night sleeping on a pile of jute sacks.
The next morning, he apprenticed himself to an elderly carpenter named Master Dawood. Dawood taught him to plane cedar timber, handle the saw, and carve mortise-and-tenon joints.

For three years, Mohammed lived among working men. He learned the value of a hard-earned loaf of bread, the sorrow of an artisan whose child falls sick without medicine, and the quiet dignity of a community that shares its crusts.
His body grew strong, his mind alert, and his heart filled with deep empathy for the toiling multitudes. With his savings, he carved beautiful wooden ship-fittings that merchants bought with eager praise.

At last, with a leather purse filled with gold dinars earned by his carpentry, Mohammed returned to his father's palace.
He knelt before the throne, not in silk, but in his carpenter's apron, presenting the purse:
'Father, I return not as an idle prince, but as a man who knows how bread is won and how a kingdom's true wealth resides in the hands of its craftsmen.'

Tears of profound joy streamed down Sultan Shams al-Din's cheeks. He embraced his son:
'Now, Mohammed, thou art worthy to wear the crown. For he who has never bent his back to work cannot know how to lift the burdens of his people.'

Mohammed succeeded his father, ruling India with legendary justice, lowering taxes on working artisans, and building schools for the children of laborers.
moral: A ruler's son must learn the dignity of manual labor and honest hardship before he is fit to wear a crown.
